purpose: Fluorouracil is used to treat certain types of cancer, including colon, rectal, breast, stomach, and pancreatic cancers when given as an injection. As a cream, it is used to treat pre-cancerous skin spots (called actinic keratoses) and certain types of skin cancer. Your doctor will choose the form that is best suited for your condition.
how_it_works: Cancer cells grow and divide very quickly. Fluorouracil works by sneaking into cancer cells and blocking them from making the building blocks they need to copy their DNA. Without these building blocks, the cancer cells cannot multiply and they eventually die. Think of it like putting the wrong key into a lock — the cancer cells get stuck and cannot keep growing.
common_side_effects: When used as a cream: redness, burning, peeling, irritation, and sensitivity in the treated skin area — this is actually a normal sign the medicine is working. When given by injection or IV: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, mouth sores, loss of appetite, hair thinning, and feeling tired or weak. Most side effects improve after treatment ends.
warnings: Tell your doctor right away if you have severe diarrhea, mouth sores that prevent eating or drinking, chest pain, signs of infection (fever, chills), or unusual bruising or bleeding. Do not apply the cream near your eyes, mouth, or nose. If you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, talk to your doctor first, as this medicine can harm an unborn baby. Avoid sun exposure on treated skin areas. Always wash your hands after applying the cream.
typical_dosing: The dose depends on what condition is being treated and whether you are using the cream or the IV form. The cream is usually applied once or twice a day to the affected skin area for several weeks. IV doses are given in cycles by a healthcare provider in a clinic or hospital and are carefully calculated based on your body size and overall health. Never change your dose on your own — always follow your doctor's instructions exactly.
